entry:
Span of human history in the Americas from the initial peopling of the continents to the onset of European colonization, which began with [[Christopher Columbus]]'s voyage in 1492. Also called the pre-contact, pre-Hispanic, or (in Brazil) pre-Cabraline era, it covers Indigenous cultures before significant European influence, which in some places did not arrive until decades or even centuries after 1492.

Asian nomads, termed [[Paleo-Indians]], are thought to have entered the Americas by way of [[Beringia]], the now-submerged land bridge, and possibly along the coast, then spread southward. The date is debated: [[Clovis culture]] sites are some 13,000 years old, but older sites, to 20,000 years ago, have been claimed. A short chronology places the first movement beyond Alaska no earlier than 14,000–17,000 years ago; a long chronology proposes 30,000–40,000 years ago or earlier.

Many societies developed permanent settlements, cities, agriculture, monumental architecture, major earthworks, and complex hierarchies. Domesticated crops included [[Maize|maize]], potatoes, and quinoa. The mound-building Mississippians raised ceremonial complexes such as [[Cahokia]]; the [[Maya civilization|Maya]] had a hieroglyphic script, precise calendars, and stepped pyramids; and the [[Inca Empire]] built roads totaling over 40,000 km. Warfare, slavery, and large-scale human sacrifice are also documented in some of these societies.

Some civilizations had declined by the time of the first permanent European colonies and are known mainly through archaeology and oral histories; others were recorded in European accounts. Many Maya records were destroyed by Christian Europeans such as Diego de Landa, who viewed them as pagan yet sought to preserve native histories; a few originals survive. Study is now multidisciplinary, with 19th-century archaeology prompting reconsideration of early European sources.

Process of mass reproducing text and images from a master form or template, by transferring ink to a surface such as paper. The earliest known form evolved from ink rubbings made on paper or cloth from texts on stone tablets in the sixth century, and printing by pressing an inked image onto paper ([[Woodblock printing|woodblock printing]]) appeared later that century. Mechanical woodblock printing on paper began in the 7th century under the [[Tang dynasty]] and spread throughout East Asia. The first completely surviving printed book is the [[Diamond Sutra]] of 868, uncovered at Dunhuang.

From 900 to 1444, wooden and tin block printing was used throughout the Islamic world for amulets, tax receipts, state decrees, and paper money, then vanished without explanation. In Europe, block printing arrived as a method of printing on cloth, common by 1300; once paper became easily available around 1400, it passed quickly to woodcut religious images and playing cards, produced in very large numbers from about 1425.

[[Movable type]] allowed far more flexible processes than hand copying or block printing. [[Bi Sheng]] created the first known system in China around 1040, using clay type; woodblock printing nevertheless remained cheaper for Chinese, with its thousands of characters. In Korea, the *Jikji* (1377) is the earliest extant book produced with metal movable type. [[Johannes Gutenberg]]'s [[Printing press|printing press]] of around 1450 combined cast metal type with a screw mechanism; the Gutenberg Bible was printed c. 1455. Printing is credited with a key role in the Renaissance and the [[Scientific Revolution]]. Offset lithography now serves commercial volumes, and digital techniques serve on-demand production.

Condition or claim of an individual or group to be free from unwanted access, observation, or disclosure, and to determine how far they, and information about them, are exposed to others. The concept has no single accepted definition. Lawyers, philosophers, and social scientists have understood it as a right to be let alone, as limited access to the self, as secrecy, as control over personal information, as a precondition of personhood and intimate relationships, and as the appropriate flow of information within social contexts.

Distinctions between public and private life appear in many ancient societies, but privacy emerged as a distinct legal claim only in the 19th century, when printing and photographic technologies and the popular press prompted calls for protection. In "The Right to Privacy" (1890), Samuel D. Warren and [[Louis Brandeis]] argued that the common law should recognize a general "right to be let alone." In the second half of the 20th century, computers shifted attention to the collection and processing of personal data, producing data protection law that began in Western Europe in the 1970s and has spread worldwide.

Privacy is protected as a human right by Article 12 of the [[Universal Declaration of Human Rights]], Article 17 of the [[International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights]], and regional instruments such as Article 8 of the [[European Convention on Human Rights]]. Protection differs by jurisdiction: European law tends to treat privacy as an aspect of personal dignity and comprehensively regulates personal data, whereas U.S. law has traditionally emphasized liberty against the state and regulates the private sector by sector. Digital technologies have intensified debate over [[Surveillance|surveillance]] by governments and corporations; responses include legislation, litigation, and tools such as [[Encryption|encryption]].

G-type main-sequence star (G2V) at the center of the [[Solar System]], the main source of energy for life on Earth. A massive sphere of hot plasma, it is heated to incandescence by [[Nuclear fusion|nuclear fusion]] in its core and radiates mainly visible light and infrared radiation, with 10% at ultraviolet energies. It has been an object of veneration in many cultures and a central subject of astronomical research since antiquity; its scientific study is called heliology.

The Sun orbits the Galactic Center at a distance of 24,000 to 28,000 light-years. Its mean distance from Earth, about 1.496 × 10⁸ km or 8 light-minutes, defined the [[Astronomical unit|astronomical unit]], now fixed at 149,597,870.7 km. It is the largest and most massive object in the Solar System: its diameter is about 1,391,400 km, around 109 times Earth's, and its mass is around 330,000 times Earth's, about 99.86% of the system's total. It has no definite boundary; density falls exponentially with height above the [[Photosphere|photosphere]], the apparent visible surface that defines its radius. Its oblateness is only 8.2 × 10⁻⁶ (8 parts per million), making it the natural object closest to a perfect sphere ever observed. Its absolute magnitude of +4.83 makes it brighter than about 85% of the stars in the Milky Way, most of which are red dwarfs. It is a Population I, heavy-element-rich star.

By mass, the photosphere is 74.9% hydrogen and 23.8% helium; heavier elements account for under 2%, chiefly oxygen (roughly 1%), carbon (0.3%), neon (0.2%), and iron (0.2%). Each second the core fuses about 600 billion kg of hydrogen into helium, converting four billion kg of matter into energy. The photosphere has an effective temperature of 5,772 K, and the corona reaches up to 2 million °C. The Sun rotates faster at its equator than at its poles, with a period relative to the stars of about 25.6 days at the equator and 33.5 days at the poles, counterclockwise as seen from above its north pole. The early Sun may have rotated up to ten times faster; magnetic braking, as its magnetic field interacted with the outflowing [[Solar wind|solar wind]], slowed it. [[Sunspot|Sunspots]], flares, and coronal mass ejections follow an approximately 11-year magnetic activity cycle and affect space weather and satellite operations.

The Sun formed about 4.6 billion years ago from the gravitational collapse of matter within a large molecular cloud; most of the matter gathered at the center, and the rest flattened into a disk that became the Solar System. In about four to seven billion years, as core hydrogen fusion diminishes, its outer layers will expand and it will become a [[Red giant|red giant]]. Models suggest it will then shed its outer layers and become a [[White dwarf|white dwarf]], glowing for perhaps trillions of years, and is theorized to end as a black dwarf giving off negligible energy.

The English word *sun* derives from Old English *sunne*, from Proto-Germanic *sunnōn*, related to Latin *sōl* and ancient Greek *hēlios*, from which come the adjectives *solar* and *heliac*.

Transmission of information over a distance by electrical, electronic, or other electromagnetic means, typically through cables, radio waves, or optical systems. Channels may be divided for multiplexing, allowing one medium to carry several concurrent sessions. The French engineer and novelist Édouard Estaunié coined the term in 1904, defining it as "remote transmission of thought through electricity". The [[International Telecommunication Union]] definition excludes slow technologies such as postal mail and pneumatic tubes.

Earlier long-distance methods included smoke signals, beacons, and signal flags. [[Homing pigeon|Homing pigeons]] were used in Ancient Persia and by the Roman Empire. Beacon chains could pass only a single bit of information, as during the Spanish Armada, when one relayed a signal from Plymouth to London. In 1792 Claude Chappe built the first fixed visual telegraph line, between Lille and Paris; the last commercial semaphore line was abandoned in 1880 in the face of electrical competition.

On July 25, 1837, William Fothergill Cooke and [[Charles Wheatstone]] demonstrated the first commercial [[Electrical telegraph|electrical telegraph]]; [[Samuel Morse]] independently developed a version whose code was an important advance. Developers of the telephone include Antonio Meucci, Philipp Reis, Elisha Gray, and [[Alexander Graham Bell]]. Wireless communication began a revolution in the first decade of the 20th century with the radio work of [[Guglielmo Marconi]], who won the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics. Since the 1960s digital technologies have supplemented voice with data, optical fibre has overcome limits of metal media, and the [[Internet]] has given global access independent of any given medium.

In the United States, AT&T dominated infrastructure until its 1984 breakup. Regulation has since shifted toward liberalization, while debate continues over whether network deployment tends toward natural monopoly and over the need for antitrust oversight.
